extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluation criteria for designing, constructing, launching, steering, recording experiments with, and competing model aeroplanes (rubber-, steam- or petrol-driven). Emphasis on materials, balance, aerofoil design, propellers, motors, steering, launching, record-keeping and competition metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material selection — strength-for-weight superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: A substance must be 'lighter and stronger weight for weight' to be superior for aeronautical purpose; slight differences may be decided by bulk and resulting air resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steel generally outperforms aluminium and magnalium despite being heavier because it is much stronger weight-for-weight; aluminium and magnalium permissible breaking strengths cited (60% and 80% respectively), whereas steel can be given 80% and is superior in section (less resistance). Weight ratios given (magnalium:aluminium :: 8:9). Choose materials according to strength-to-weight and bulk (air resistance) considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limitations of sheet materials and woods
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation of sheet ebonite, vulcanized fibre, sheet celluloid (but note brittleness), and specific woods (Lombardy poplar, Honduras mahogany, beech, ash) for parts such as small propellers and aerofoils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sheet ebonite and vulcanized fibre useful for small propellers; sheet celluloid can be used but becomes brittle and shrinks; avoid mica. Jointless cane useful for main aerofoil, skids, etc. Three-, four- and five-ply woods are available providing great strength and lightness. Lombardy poplar is light (increasing bulk/air resistance), Honduras mahogany is a better all-round wood; ash high in resilience. Hollow reeds and porcupine quills can be used for extreme lightness. Consider resilience and stiffness trade-offs (footnote: cane's want of stiffness can be a disadvantage where stiffness with resilience is required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve structural continuity; reinforce drilled/thinned members
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not interrupt continuity of any rib, tube, spar, etc., by drilling holes or thinning holding places; if interrupted, add reinforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If continuity must be interrupted, impart additional strength by binding (with thread, not wire), or slipping a slightly larger tube over the other. Avoid making parts excessively thin where strength is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design progression: start simple (monoplane) then advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by making a simple monoplane and proceed to more elaborate scientific models as skill increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The actual building is not so difficult, but design is hard; start simple to learn fundamentals before attempting complex designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential skills: learn to solder
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning to solder is absolutely essential for model construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soldering skill is required for fittings and joins; use as little solder as possible where indicated in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller placement: rear (pusher) preferred over tractor (front)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid tractor screw-main plane in front and tail behind (Blériot type); the proper place for the propeller is behind, in the wake of the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: difficulty getting centre of gravity forward with tractor layout; front screw strikes machine with backwash causing retardation and disturbed air under/over aerofoil — undisturbed air is required for proper lifting effect. Rear placement recovers some energy lost to resistance and can reduce slip; front-mounted screws also expose main aerofoil first to gusts, harder for elevator to rectify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerofoil covering material choice by model size
rubrics_metrics.description: Wooden or metal aerofoils are more efficient than fabric-covered ones but are satisfactory only in smaller sizes; larger-sized models should use fabric-covered aerofoils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wood/metal rely on speed and are prone to hard smash at landing due to higher necessary speed; fabric-covered types sustain flight at lower speeds and are preferred for larger models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable aerofoil shapes and fabric-stretching technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Only three aerofoil planforms need be considered: (a) rectangular, (b) elongated ellipse, (c) chamfered rear edge. Fabric must be stretched with correct longitudinal and transverse tension to achieve the desired aerocurve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example method: bend pianoforte wire into a soldered circle, stitch silk/nainsook over it while deforming to elliptical shape to create double curvature; regulate transverse (dihedral) by cross threads/wires; longitudinal camber regulated by initial tension and method of fixing to framework. Use thin rubber cord binding as a shock-absorbing, slightly flexible fastener to the main framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use flexible joints and proper stays in biplanes
rubrics_metrics.description: Flexible joints are advantageous in biplanes and rigidity is obtained by steel wire stays or thin silk cord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexible joints can be made using wire hooks and eyes and held by binding with silk/thread; use steel stays where rigidity is needed and silk/thin cord where lighter stays suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-surface aerofoils on very small scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-surface aerofoils are not desirable for very small scale models except on large size power-driven models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra weight and construction difficulties at small scale make double-surface unnecessary and often counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motor mounting: isolate rubber motor from elevator outriggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not connect the rod/tube carrying the rubber motor with the outrigger carrying the elevator; torque of rubber twists the framework and interferes with elevator action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If connection is unavoidable, the rod must be stayed with piano wire both longitudinally (to overcome large pull) and laterally (to overcome torque).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining and adjusting balance: centre of gravity and centre of pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Balancing point is usually slightly in front or just within the front edge of the main aerofoil; adjust rod carrying rubber motor and propeller until best balance is obtained and hang up machine to ascertain centre of gravity (approximately centre of pressure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust component locations to achieve the indicated balance; experimentation required. In Clarke models centre of pressure slightly in front of main plane when small front plane used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevator as non-lifting balancer
rubrics_metrics.description: Elevator (tail) should be of non-lifting type—the entire weight should be carried by the main aerofoil and the elevator used simply as a balancer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If elevator carries weight then it must be larger or set at a large angle, both increasing resistance and reducing efficiency. This practice implies placing propeller some distance behind main supporting surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undercarriage: use skids, not wheels, for flying models
rubrics_metrics.description: In actual flying models skids should be used instead of wheels; wheels require large diameter and are too heavy to be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skids can be made from cane, imitation whalebone, steel springs, pianoforte wire; steel pianoforte wire best. For larger models bamboo or ash/strong cane suitable. Use shock absorbers (steel wire loops, whalebone, steel springs) lashed by thin india-rubber cord to allow 'give' in multiple directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biplane gap and interference considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In biplanes the 'gap' must not be less than the 'chord'—preferably greater. In double monoplanes (Langley type) there is interference where the rear plane moves in air acted on by the front one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference decreases efficiency and can be partially overcome by varying dihedral angle or placing planes far apart. In biplanes without dihedral, the propeller may be placed slightly to one side to neutralise torque; best position determined by experiment unless pitch is very large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design objective trade-offs: distance vs duration
rubrics_metrics.description: For longest possible distance choose monoplane type; for maximum time aloft choose biplane or triplane. For longest flight twin propellers rotating in opposite directions are ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: adding a second propeller (and rubber) increased weight by 20% but resistance by ~10% yielding a net gain in performance (~70% gain in the writer's example). Using geared motors can allow more bunches of rubber for more turns. Keep number of strands and gearing in mind; aim for at least ~1000 turns from strands length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller and aerofoil geometry recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Propellers should be of large diameter and pitch (not less than 35° at the tips), of curved shape; aerofoil surface of as high an aspect ratio as possible, and slight camber if any.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wind-cambered surfaces may help in steady winds but are unsuitable in gusty weather where the wind may camber the surface the wrong way. Oiled or specially prepared light silk recommended for surfacing. For wooden/metal aerofoils favour high speed designs; for long-duration flat or very slight camber surfaces may perform best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise weight; overall proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Weight should be an absolute minimum and everything not essential omitted. Total length of model should be at least twice the span of the main aerofoil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended practical experiment weight range ~5 oz to 10 oz for balance between buildability and delicacy. 'One-ouncers' and extremely light models can achieve long flights but are harder to build.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubber motor design and winding practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of rubber strands should permit at least a thousand turns; a winder is essential. For twin motors, wind both propellers at the same time using a double winder to avoid unequal torsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number of strands, kind (flat, square or round), length, number of turns, and condition at end of flight are important experimental variables (see Experimental Data form). Gear trains may be used to increase available turns but add weight. For twin motors, test equality by weighing strands and ensure equal friction and simultaneous release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steering: causes and corrective strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary steering problems arise from propeller torque and varying air currents; multiple devices exist to counteract these effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include: (a) offsetting the motor rod slightly from main aerofoil centre (monoplane); (b) in biplanes placing bearing bracket at right angles horizontally to rod; (c) using two equal propellers of opposite pitch and equal rubber motors (theoretically perfect but practically difficult unless wound and released identically); (d) vertical fins placed rear above CG (not large); (e) small balancing tips/ailerons near main aerofoil; (f) canting by weighting a tip (clumsy); (g) using elevator mounted on universal joint allowing tipping and canting; (h) vertical fin or keel down backbone. Emphasise testing and experimentation to find optimal positions and settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torque balancing and testing procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is vital to balance propeller torque as far as possible; test and adjust experimentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by balancing model transversely on a knife edge, wind up propeller and let run down, and adjust until torque and compensatory apparatus balance (use the mean torque if it varies). For twin propellers suspend by CG, wind up both and observe whether model is drawn forward without rotation; if not, adjust (e.g., place stronger propeller slightly nearer the centre). For counter-rotating concentric shafts, the rear propeller operating in already-driven air will need coarser pitch or larger diameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use speed to overcome air-current steering disturbances
rubrics_metrics.description: The best (and only reliable) way to overcome air currents of varying velocity/direction is speed — give the aeroplane high velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target velocities of 20–30 miles per hour (attainable in petrol/steam-driven or wooden/metal aerofoil models). Higher speed reduces deviations from course caused by gusts and currents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Launching: basic rules and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should generally be launched against the wind and with an initial velocity near their flight velocity; launch angle should be horizontal or only slightly inclined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Featherweight long-flight models designed for flying with the wind should be launched with the wind; models needing high initial velocity (wooden/metal high-aspect) may need to be hurled. For rubber-driven models intended to take off under own power, required ground run should be short (10–12 ft max). Do not tip elevator at large angle on ground unless a mechanical device reduces angle at release. Propeller selection for take-off: high statical-thrust propellers preferred; small fine-pitch props start quickly but are less efficient in flight. For twin-screw models, hold brackets so propellers don't revolve, raise and push forward then release both simultaneously (recommended alternative technique holding by a centre rod at CG and releasing propellers briefly before launching). Allowing propellers to run briefly (about 1 second) before release may give steadier initial flight. Use smooth oilcloth or plank to assist ground run; never launch by one hand only unless the special one-handed technique is described carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helicopter-specific layout rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For model helicopters the horizontal propulsive thrust must be in the same plane as the vertical lift; otherwise the model will somersault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider using superimposed counter-rotating screws for torque resistance; horizontal revolving propellers for propulsion will have increased lifting power when advancing on fresh undisturbed air. Lightweight wire framework fabric-covered screws may be suitable when thrust must exceed total weight. Alternatives: use gearing to turn torque through right angle for lifting screws and separate rubber strands for multiple propellers. Include vertical fin/keel for directional stability; four-propeller arrangements (two lift, two drift) are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep accurate experimental records; recommended data fields
rubrics_metrics.description: A model flying machine is a scientific invention — keep accurate records and share them. The book provides Experimental Data Form I with column headings of key metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form I column headings (first table): Model; Weight; Area of Supporting Surface; Aspect Ratio; Average Length of Flight (ft); Maximum Flight; Time of Flight (average and maximum); Kind and Direction of Wind; Camber; Angle of Inclination of Main Aerofoil to Line of Flight. Continued columns: Weight of (Rubber) Motor; Kind of Rubber (flat/square/round); Length in inches and number of strands; Number of Turns; Condition at End of Flight; Number of Propellers and Diameter; Number of Blades; Disc Area and Pitch; Percentage of Slip; Thrust; Torque in inch-ounces. Guidance: vary forms at reader's discretion, supply data to aeronautical journals when carefully arranged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition criteria and classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative model-flying competition tests include longest flight, stability (longitudinal and transverse), longest glide (launched from a given height without power but with motor/propeller attached), steering, greatest height, and best all-round model including excellence in building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: marks allotted per test, aggregate points determine winners; separate prizes may be offered for longest flight, swiftest flight over a measured distance, greatest height, stability and steering, and best all-round. Models divided into classes by supporting surface (e.g., A: 1 sq. ft. and under; B: 2 sq. ft.; C: 4 sq. ft.; D: 8 sq. ft.; E: ...).
